title: Two club rosters
topic: A friend subtracts two overlapping club sizes without knowing the overlap
blurb: They admit they have zero idea how many people are in both clubs — then quote an exact gap.
prompt: A friend sent this while organizing two neighborhood clubs. Tap a line if the logic breaks, or call it clean.

segments.label: The counts
segments.text: Counted up our neighborhood running and board-game rosters — 64 people are in the running club and 41 are in board games.

segments.label: The mess
segments.text: I have no idea how many people are in both clubs, because half the group uses nicknames on the signup sheet.

segments.label: The gap
segments.text: Still, the number of people who only run is definitely 23 more than the number who only play board games.

segments.label: The shortcut
segments.text: I don't even need to deduplicate the spreadsheet to know that gap is 23.

conclusion: Without knowing how many people are in both clubs, run-only members still outnumber board-game-only members by exactly 23.

diagnosis: 64 plus 41 is 105, which double-counts everyone in both clubs, so those two totals can't be compared directly.
Because nicknames let one person sign up twice in the same club, 64 and 41 aren't clean headcounts.
The two clubs have different sizes, so you should compare percentages rather than raw headcounts.
Without knowing the total number of neighbors in the building, 64 and 41 leave out non-members.
fix: Match real names across both sheets before comparing 64 and 41.
Wait until you have the combined unique headcount before subtracting anything.
Convert 64 and 41 into shares of the neighborhood instead of raw counts.
Remove anyone who hasn't attended in the last month before counting.

diagnosis: If you don't know the overlap, you have two unknowns and only one equation, so the exclusive counts are unsolvable.
Nicknames only matter if more than 23 people are in both clubs — up to 23, the gap stays positive.
Admitting you don't know the overlap makes any exact number in line 3 a guess.
Every person in both clubs sits inside both 64 and 41, which shrinks the gap every time someone joins both.
fix: Deduplicate the nicknames first so you can subtract the overlap from 64 and 41.
Report a range for the gap (between 0 and 23) instead of pinning it to 23.
Ask members to confirm their real names before stating any 'only' counts.
Assume at least 10–15 people overlap and reduce the 23 accordingly.

diagnosis: You can't subtract 64 minus 41 to get the 'only' gap — everyone in both clubs is double-counted and changes the difference.
23 is the gap between *total* runners and *total* gamers, not between *only*-runners and *only*-gamers.
If 20 people are in both clubs, you have to subtract 20 from the 23 gap, leaving only 3.
You can only say run-only is *at least* 23 more; if nobody overlaps it's 23, otherwise it shrinks.
fix: Say the gap between run-only and board-game-only is at most 23, depending on the overlap.
Subtract the overlap once from 23 as soon as you find out how many people are in both.
Change 'only run vs only board games' to 'total running vs total board games'.
Wait to count the overlap — every shared member cuts the gap by 2.

diagnosis: You definitely need to deduplicate the sheet first, because the overlap could swing the gap anywhere from 0 to 41.
Skipping deduplication only works for the *sum* of both clubs, not for the difference of exclusive members.
Even if the gap happens to be 23 on average, you can't claim it 'definitely' without checking the sheet.
If all 41 board gamers also run, there are 0 board-game-only members, which breaks the subtraction.
fix: Deduplicate the sheet before quoting any exact difference.
Check the edge case where all 41 gamers also run before claiming 23 always holds.
Only skip deduplication if you're reporting the raw 64 vs 41 totals.
Estimate the overlap with a quick poll in the chat first.

clean_segments: Counted up our neighborhood running and board-game rosters — 64 people are in the running club and 41 are in board games.
I have no idea how many people are in both clubs, because half the group uses nicknames on the signup sheet.
Still, the number of people who only run is definitely 23 more than the number who only play board games.
I don't even need to deduplicate the spreadsheet to know that gap is 23.
clean_conclusion: The unknown overlap cancels right out: if k people are in both clubs, run-only is 64 − k and board-game-only is 41 − k. Subtract them and k vanishes — the gap is 23 whether k is 0 or 41.
explanation: The unknown overlap cancels right out: if k people are in both clubs, run-only is 64 − k and board-game-only is 41 − k. Subtract them and k vanishes — the gap is 23 whether k is 0 or 41.
